buildUp: To reach 300 m without enormous weight, you need a material strong for its weight and a shape that wastes none of it, so the tower is wrought iron, arranged as an open lattice.
Wind's toppling effect grows towards the ground, so the structure splits into four legs that curve outwards, each landing on its own masonry pier.
Each leg is a box of four curved corner girders braced by lattice, so it acts as a stiff column and the wind's push is shared between the girders on both sides.
The legs lean in and meet, first tied together by a belt of girders at the first floor at about 57 m, then joined into one shaft at the second floor at about 116 m.
Above that, one tapering shaft with a girder at each corner rises to the top floor at about 276 m, getting slimmer as the wind's toppling effect above it gets smaller.
To bring visitors up, lifts ride inclined tracks up the curving legs, a vertical lift climbs the central shaft, and decorative arches dress the base while carrying almost no load.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Build it as an open iron lattice whose shape follows the forces that wind puts on it. Wind blows through the gaps instead of pushing on a solid wall, and the four legs curve outwards at the bottom just as much as the wind's toppling effect demands, so every girder is simply squeezed or pulled along its length rather than bent. The result is enormously tall for remarkably little metal.

hardParts.title: Making four leaning legs meet in mid-air
hardParts.why: Each leg leaned out unsupported as it grew, held up by temporary wooden towers and sand boxes, and all four had to meet the first floor girders about 57 m up within a tiny margin. Hydraulic jacks in the iron shoes on the piers let the builders nudge each leg by millimetres until everything lined up level.

hardParts.title: Thousands of parts that had to fit first time
hardParts.why: Every one of the tower's roughly 18,000 iron pieces was drawn, cut and drilled in Eiffel's workshop before it arrived, so on site the teams could only rivet, not reshape. Joining them took some 2.5 million rivets. A mistake in the drawings would have shown up as holes that didn't line up hundreds of metres in the air.

hardParts.title: Lifts that climb a curve
hardParts.why: Because the legs curve, an ordinary vertical lift can't run up them. The leg lifts ride inclined tracks whose slope changes as they climb, while the cabin must stay level for passengers, and in 1889 this needed new machinery. The tower's height also forced the trip to be split into stages.

principles.explanation: The wind's toppling effect is greatest near the ground, so the tower's legs spread furthest apart there, about 125 m across at the base, while the top stays narrow. Wind presses on anything in its way with a force that grows with the square of its speed: a strong gale of about 150 km/h pushes with roughly 100 kg on every square metre it hits. On a tall tower, that push acts like a hand at the top of a lever, and its toppling effect builds up the further down you go. An open lattice also lets most of the wind through, so there's much less to push on in the first place.
principles.title: Wind, not weight, sets the shape

principles.explanation: The curved legs and criss-cross lattice make the forces from wind and weight run straight along each girder, so the iron is pulled or squeezed rather than bent. A thin iron bar is very strong when you pull or squeeze it along its length, but weak when you bend it, the way a ruler is hard to stretch but easy to flex. So Eiffel's engineers curved the legs to follow those forces, and because a triangle of bars can't change shape without stretching or squashing one of them, the criss-cross lattice turns every load into pushes and pulls the bars handle well.
principles.title: Push and pull, but don't bend

principles.explanation: Because almost every piece of iron works efficiently, the whole tower weighs only about 7,300 tonnes. Melted down and spread over the square under its legs, about 125 m across, that iron would make a slab only about 6 cm thick. That lightness also means the masonry piers press on the ground surprisingly gently, which mattered on the sandy, damp soil beside the Seine.
principles.title: Light for its size

principles.explanation: On a hot day the sunny side of the tower grows a little longer than the shaded side, so the top leans gently away from the sun, by up to about 15 to 18 cm. That's because iron expands by about 12 millionths of its length for every degree it warms. A lattice of riveted iron can flex this way day after day without harm, as long as rust is kept away from it.
principles.title: Iron moves with the sun

firstPrinciples.problem: Build something 300 m tall, nearly twice the height of anything standing in 1889, in about two years, with the materials and cranes of the time, in the middle of a city. A tall structure's real enemy isn't its own weight but the wind, which pushes harder the higher you go and tries to topple the whole thing over its base. It had to be strong and stiff enough to stand in a gale, light enough not to crush its foundations, and cheap and quick enough to build for a fair.

questions.answer: The wind's toppling effect adds up with height, so it is largest at the base. Spreading the legs widest there gives them the leverage to resist it, while near the top only a little wind is pushing above, so a slim shaft is enough.
questions.question: Why is the tower so much wider at the bottom than at the top?

questions.answer: A solid tower would catch the full force of the wind and need far more material to resist it. The open lattice lets most of the wind through, so the iron only has to carry the push on the bars themselves.
questions.question: Why is the tower an open lattice instead of solid walls?

questions.answer: The sunny side warms up and expands more than the shaded side. Being slightly longer, the sunny side pushes the top over towards the cooler side, by up to about 15 to 18 cm.
questions.question: Why does the top of the tower lean away from the sun on a hot day?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The tower looks decorative, but its famous outline is really a diagram of the forces acting on it. Instead of resisting wind with mass, as stone towers do, it lets the wind through and shapes the remaining iron to carry what's left with pure push and pull. That let Eiffel's team nearly double the height of anything built before, using a modest amount of iron in about two years.

name: Eiffel Tower
overview:
The Eiffel Tower was built in just over two years for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, the World's Fair marking a century since the French Revolution. Designed by the engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier and the architect Stephen Sauvestre at Gustave Eiffel's company, it was the tallest structure in the world for 41 years. It was meant to stand for only 20; it survived because its height made it useful for radio.

It's a wind-shaped lattice. Four huge legs, each a curved box of iron girders, rise from masonry foundations and lean in to meet in a single tapering tower. Their curve follows the forces that wind puts on the tower, so the open lattice lets air through and the whole thing weighs surprisingly little for its size: about 7,300 tonnes of iron, less than the air in a box the same size. The decorative arches between the legs carry almost no load.

Visitors climb or ride up to three levels: the first floor at 57 m, the second at 116 m and the top at 276 m, where Eiffel kept a small apartment. Lifts run up the curving legs on inclined tracks, and today antennas on the very top broadcast radio and television across Paris. The tower is repainted by hand about every seven years to stop it rusting.

parts.description: Block of limestone and concrete under each leg corner, spreading the leg's weight into the ground.

details.didYouKnow: The two legs nearest the Seine sit on wetter ground, so their foundations were dug inside sealed iron boxes pumped full of compressed air to keep river water out while men worked below.
details.howItWorks: Each leg ends in iron shoes that sit on solid masonry blocks, so the curved corner girders press straight down into stone rather than onto soil. The blocks spread the load over a wide area, keeping the pressure on the ground surprisingly gentle. During building, hydraulic jacks set into the shoes let engineers raise or lower each leg slightly so all four met the first floor girders perfectly level.
keyNumbers: About 125 m between the outer corners of the base
Construction began on the foundations in about January 1887
Pressure on the soil roughly like a person sitting on a chair
details.madeOf: Cut limestone blocks laid on beds of concrete. Stone and concrete are excellent in compression and do not rust, which suits a part that only ever gets pushed down on and sits close to damp ground.

parts.name: Masonry foundation pier

parts.description: Cast-iron shoes where each corner girder lands on its masonry, with pockets where hydraulic jacks levelled the legs.

details.didYouKnow: The legs were set out so precisely that, when the first-floor girders were finally lifted into place in 1888, they joined up with only tiny corrections from the jacks.
details.howItWorks: Each corner girder ends in an iron shoe bolted down onto its masonry block, so its load passes into stone over a wide, flat seat. While the legs were being built, hydraulic jacks set into the shoes could raise or lower each girder by tiny amounts. That let the builders bring all four legs level with each other before they were joined at the first floor, after which the jacks were replaced by fixed steel wedges.
keyNumbers: One shoe under each of 16 corner girders
Adjustments of a few millimetres at a time
details.madeOf: Cast iron and wrought iron, held down by long anchor bolts set deep into the masonry. Cast iron is strong in compression, which is all a shoe ever has to resist.

parts.name: Leg shoes & jacks

parts.description: Outer corner girder of a leg, the curved edge you see in every photograph; it follows the line of wind forces down to the ground.

details.didYouKnow: While the legs were being built they leaned out unsupported, so wooden scaffolding towers and sand boxes propped them up until they could be joined at the first floor.
details.howItWorks: This is one of the two girders on the outside face of a leg, and its sweeping curve is the tower's signature line. Eiffel's engineers shaped the curve so that the forces from wind pushing on the tower run down through the legs and into the foundations without bending them. It joins the other corner girders through lattice bracing and, higher up, the horizontal belt of girders under the first floor.
keyNumbers: About 57 m of climb to the first floor
Rises roughly 116 m before the legs merge into one shaft
One of 16 corner girders across the four legs
details.madeOf: Puddled iron, a very pure wrought iron worked by hand in the furnace. It is tough and forgiving rather than brittle, and the real girder is a riveted box built up from plates and angle sections, simplified here into a single bar.

parts.name: Leg corner girder (outer)

parts.description: The other outer corner girder of the leg.

details.didYouKnow: Every hole for every rivet was drilled in Eiffel's workshop at Levallois-Perret before delivery, so pieces arrived ready to bolt and rivet with almost no fitting on site.
details.howItWorks: The second outer corner girder forms the other edge of the leg's outward-facing side, so together the pair frames the face you see from the street. Because the two outer girders splay apart at the base and close in as they rise, each leg is widest at the ground where loads are greatest. Lattice bars between them stop either one from buckling sideways.
keyNumbers: Each leg roughly 25 m across at its foot
Rests on its own masonry block
Part of about 7,300 tonnes of ironwork
details.madeOf: Puddled iron plates and angles joined by hot-driven rivets. In reality it is a hollow box girder, which gives a lot of stiffness for little weight.

parts.name: Leg corner girder (outer (second))

parts.description: Inner corner girder of a leg, facing the middle of the tower.

details.didYouKnow: Hydraulic jacks under the legs could nudge them by millimetres, letting the builders bring all four legs to the first floor girders with very little error.
details.howItWorks: The inner corner girders face the middle of the tower and are the ones that meet the great horizontal girders carrying the first floor. They curve more gently than you might expect, leaning in to meet their partners from the other legs. Getting the four inner sets to line up at about 57 m up was the trickiest moment of construction.
keyNumbers: About 57 m up to where it meets the first floor girders
Legs joined at the first floor by about early 1888
Some 2.5 million rivets in the whole tower
details.madeOf: Puddled iron box girder, riveted from flat plates and angle sections. Wrought iron was chosen over cast iron because it copes well with the pulling forces that wind creates on the inward side.

parts.name: Leg corner girder (inner)

parts.description: The other inner corner girder of the leg.

details.didYouKnow: Rivets were heated red hot and hammered in by teams of about four men; as each rivet cooled it shrank and pulled the plates tightly together.
details.howItWorks: This second inner girder completes the box-shaped leg, so each leg is really a tall, tapering four-sided column. With its partner it frames the inside face, which looks across the open space under the tower. When wind blows, the leeward inner girders are squeezed while those on the windward side are pulled, and the lattice shares the load between them.
keyNumbers: About 18,000 individual iron parts in the tower
Most pieces light enough for a small crane
Top of the tower sways only a few cm in wind
details.madeOf: Riveted puddled iron. Its plates were made in many small pieces light enough to lift with simple cranes, then joined in place.

parts.name: Leg corner girder (inner (second))

parts.description: Criss-cross of small iron bars bracing the leg's girders; it's what makes the tower look like lace.

details.didYouKnow: If all the tower's iron were melted down and spread over the square of its base, it would make a layer only about 6 cm thick.
details.howItWorks: On the lower outer face, these crossing bars tie the two outer corner girders together so neither can bow outward under load. The open criss-cross lets wind pass straight through instead of pushing on a solid wall, which is why such a tall tower needs so little metal. Near the base the bracing is at its largest, matching the wide spread of the leg.
keyNumbers: Spans legs up to roughly 25 m wide
Bracing below about 57 m
Repainted about every 7 years
details.madeOf: Puddled iron flats and angles riveted at every crossing. Many small, thin members are lighter than a few big ones yet still very stiff when triangulated.

parts.name: Leg lattice (lower, outer face)

parts.description: Criss-cross of small iron bars bracing the leg's girders; it's what makes the tower look like lace.

details.didYouKnow: The tower is painted in graded shades, darkest at the bottom and lightest at the top, so that it looks one even colour against the sky.
details.howItWorks: This lattice braces the inner face of a leg below the first floor, the side that looks into the great open space under the tower. It keeps the inner girders working as a team and stops the leg from twisting. It also forms part of the screen through which the leg lifts and stairs can be glimpsed as they climb.
keyNumbers: About 57 m tall up to the first floor
Open lattice faces all four legs
Roughly 60 tonnes of paint per repaint
details.madeOf: Riveted puddled iron bars. Their lacy appearance is a happy side effect of an engineering goal: as little surface as possible for the wind to push on.

parts.name: Leg lattice (lower, inner face)

parts.description: Criss-cross of small iron bars bracing the leg's girders; it's what makes the tower look like lace.

details.didYouKnow: Because the open lattice catches so little air, the tower's top moves only a few centimetres even in strong winds.
details.howItWorks: Between the first and second floors, the outer faces of the legs narrow and lean inward more steeply, and this lattice keeps them rigid. The bars are smaller here because the legs carry less weight than they do lower down. They also help pass the push of wind from the upper tower down into the leg girders.
keyNumbers: Spans roughly 57 m to 116 m up
Legs merge into one shaft at about 116 m
details.madeOf: Puddled iron, riveted. The lighter bars save weight high up, which in turn reduces the load on everything beneath.

parts.name: Leg lattice (upper, outer face)

parts.description: Criss-cross of small iron bars bracing the leg's girders; it's what makes the tower look like lace.

details.didYouKnow: On a sunny day the side facing the sun expands more than the shaded side, so the whole top of the tower leans gently away from the sun.
details.howItWorks: This bracing stiffens the inner face of each leg between the first and second floors, where the four legs bend towards each other. It works with the second floor girders to lock the legs together as they converge. Visitors riding the leg lifts pass close beside it on the way up.
keyNumbers: Spans roughly 57 m to 116 m up
About 670 steps from the ground to the second floor
Top shifts up to about 15 to 18 cm in hot sun
details.madeOf: Riveted puddled iron. Wrought iron's tolerance for repeated small movements suits a structure that flexes slightly with every gust and every sunny day.

parts.name: Leg lattice (upper, inner face)

parts.description: Great arch between two legs under the first floor; added mostly for looks and to reassure the public, it carries little load.

details.didYouKnow: Just above the arches, around the first floor, Eiffel had the names of 72 French scientists and engineers painted in large gold letters.
details.howItWorks: Each arch spans between two legs just beneath the first floor, framing the view through the tower. In Eiffel's design the real work of tying the legs together is done by the straight girders above, so the arches carry little load. Sauvestre added them to make the tower look graceful and to reassure Parisians that it was sturdy.
keyNumbers: About 74 m across between leg bases
Four arches, one on each side
Sits just under the floor at about 57 m
details.madeOf: Riveted puddled iron, like the rest of the frame. Being mostly decorative, it could be built as a lighter lattice curve.

parts.name: Decorative arch

parts.description: Lift car that climbs the curving leg on an inclined track, changing angle as it rises.

details.didYouKnow: During construction, cranes climbed the legs on the very tracks later used by the lifts, rising with the tower as it grew.
details.howItWorks: Because the legs curve, a normal vertical lift cannot climb them, so these cars run on inclined tracks whose slope changes as they rise. The cabin is built to stay level while the track gets steeper towards the top. Lifts run in three of the legs, while the south leg holds stairs and a private lift for the second floor restaurant.
keyNumbers: Climbs about 116 m to the second floor
Some machinery dates from about 1899
Built by the Fives-Lille company
details.madeOf: A steel cabin frame with glazed sides, pulled along steel rails. In the east and west legs, much of the 1899 hydraulic machinery still works, using water pressure to drive huge pistons.

parts.name: Leg lift

parts.description: Pair of rails laid up the inside of a leg, bending with its curve so a lift can climb from the ground to the second floor.

details.didYouKnow: Building lifts that climb a curve was a real challenge in 1889, and several makers, French and American, each supplied a different system for different legs.
details.howItWorks: The track runs up the inside of a leg and bends with it, so its slope steepens towards the top. A lift car riding on it must tilt its floor as it climbs to keep passengers level. Cables and pulleys, and in some legs large hydraulic pistons, haul the car up the slope and lower it back.
keyNumbers: Climbs about 116 m to the second floor
Slope changes steadily on the way up
Lifts run in three of the four legs
details.madeOf: Steel rails on iron bearers fixed to the leg's lattice. The track has to be laid to a smooth curve, because any kink would jolt the car.

parts.name: Inclined lift track

parts.description: Zigzag flights of iron stairs climbing inside a leg, landing by landing, from the ground to the first and second floors.

details.didYouKnow: Sections of the original spiral staircase to the top were removed in 1983 and later sold at auction, with some ending up in gardens and museums.
details.howItWorks: The staircases climb inside the legs in short flights joined by landings, zigzagging back and forth as the leg leans in. Walkers can go to the first and second floors this way; above that, only lifts go to the top. The flights are open iron, so you see the lattice rushing past as you climb.
keyNumbers: About 670 steps to the second floor
Roughly 330 steps to the first floor
Stairs to the top closed to the public in 1983
details.madeOf: Iron and steel stringers and treads, fixed to the leg's girders. Open treads keep the weight and wind load low.

parts.name: Leg staircase

parts.description: One side of the square first-floor platform at 57 m, with restaurants and a glass floor.

details.didYouKnow: In some winters an ice rink has been set up on the first floor, letting people skate about 57 m above Paris.
details.howItWorks: This side of the first floor sits on the massive horizontal girders that join all four legs, turning them into one stiff frame. It carries visitors, shops and restaurants around a large open square in the middle. A 2014 renovation added glass floor panels so people can look straight down to the ground.
keyNumbers: About 57 m above the ground
Several thousand square metres of floor space
Glass floor installed in about 2014
details.madeOf: An iron and steel deck structure with modern floor finishes and glass panels. The heavy girders below are original puddled iron.

parts.name: First floor deck

parts.description: Deep lattice girders ringing the first floor that tie the four legs into one frame, faced with a band of small arches.

details.didYouKnow: The names of 72 French scientists and engineers are painted in gold letters around this level, a tribute Eiffel added to the tower.
details.howItWorks: These deep lattice girders run right round the first floor, joining the four legs at about 57 m. Once they were in place the legs stopped being four separate leaning towers and became one stiff frame, which is why this belt, not the arches below, does the real structural work. On the outside a band of small arches decorates the girders.
keyNumbers: About 57 m above the ground
Several metres deep
Joined to the legs in about 1888
details.madeOf: Riveted puddled iron, built up from plates and angles into girders several metres deep. They were lifted into place piece by piece by cranes climbing the legs.

parts.name: First floor girders & frieze

parts.description: Glazed pavilion on the first floor; its glass walls give a view straight down between the legs.

details.didYouKnow: The modern pavilions were designed to use energy efficiently, with features such as solar panels and rainwater collection added during the renovation.
details.howItWorks: These glazed pavilions sit on the first floor and shelter restaurants, exhibits and visitor spaces from wind and rain. Their glass walls keep the views open while making the floor usable in all weathers. They rest on the deck rather than adding to the main structure.
keyNumbers: About 57 m up
Four pavilions around the floor
Rebuilt during the 2010s renovation
details.madeOf: Steel frames with large glass panes. Modern glazing is lighter and clearer than the heavier enclosed buildings it replaced, keeping the load on the old iron low.

parts.name: First floor gallery

parts.description: One side of the second-floor platform at 116 m, where visitors change lifts for the top.

details.didYouKnow: Eiffel used the second floor for experiments on air resistance, dropping objects on a cable to measure how air pushed on them.
details.howItWorks: The second floor is where the four legs finally come together, so this deck sits on girders that clamp them into a single base for the upper tower. Visitors arrive here by leg lift or stairs, then queue for the separate lifts to the top. It also holds the Jules Verne restaurant, reached by its own lift in the south leg.
keyNumbers: About 116 m above the ground
About 670 steps up from ground level
Roughly 160 m more to the top floor
details.madeOf: Iron and steel decking on riveted puddled iron girders. The structure must be stiff because the whole upper shaft stands on it.

parts.name: Second floor deck

parts.description: Lattice girders round the second floor that clamp the converging legs together under the upper tower.

details.didYouKnow: Building above the second floor went quickly; the upper shaft rose in about a year, and the tower was finished in March 1889.
details.howItWorks: At the second floor the legs have leaned in close together, and these girders lock them into a single base for the upper tower. They take the weight of everything above, the shaft, top floor and antenna, and pass it out to the four legs. They also stop the legs spreading apart under that load.
keyNumbers: About 116 m above the ground
Carry the whole upper tower
Roughly 160 m of tower stands on them
details.madeOf: Riveted puddled iron lattice girders, lighter than those at the first floor because the legs are smaller and closer together here.

parts.name: Second floor girders

parts.description: Corner girder of the single tapering shaft that rises from the second floor to the top.

details.didYouKnow: When it opened in 1889 the tower was the tallest structure in the world, and it kept that title for about 41 years.
details.howItWorks: From the second floor upward, the tower becomes a single tapering shaft with one corner girder at each of its four edges. The four girders lean in steadily until they meet just under the top. They carry the weight of the summit, the lifts and the antenna, as well as the strongest winds, which blow hardest high up.
keyNumbers: Rises from about 116 m to about 276 m
Four girders converging to a point
Original height about 300 m without antennas
details.madeOf: Riveted puddled iron box girders, smaller than those in the legs because there is less weight above them. Lighter pieces up high mean less load all the way down.

parts.name: Upper corner girder

parts.description: Bracing on each face of the upper shaft, stiffening it against the wind.

details.didYouKnow: Painters repaint the tower largely by hand with brushes, working from ropes and harnesses across every part of the lattice.
details.howItWorks: This bracing ties the four corner girders of the upper shaft together just above the second floor, where the shaft is at its widest. It stops the girders buckling and spreads wind loads evenly between them. It also frames the lift shaft that runs up the middle.
keyNumbers: Starts at about 116 m
About 60 tonnes of paint for the whole tower

parts.name: Upper tower lattice (lower)

parts.description: Bracing on each face of the upper shaft, stiffening it against the wind.

details.didYouKnow: The air in a cylinder just big enough to enclose the tower weighs more than all of its roughly 7,300 tonnes of iron.
details.howItWorks: Near the summit the shaft becomes slim, and this upper bracing keeps it rigid right up to the top platform. Being so high, it moves the most when the tower sways or swells in the sun, so it must stay stiff without being heavy. It hands the load of the summit structures down to the lower lattice and girders.

parts.name: Upper tower lattice (upper)

parts.description: Lift running straight up the middle of the upper shaft to the summit.

details.didYouKnow: The 1889 lift to the top was hydraulic and passengers had to change cabins halfway up at an intermediate platform.
details.howItWorks: This lift runs straight up the centre of the upper shaft from the second floor to the top. Because the shaft is vertical here, a conventional lift works without the curving tracks needed in the legs. It is the only way for the public to reach the summit, so it runs constantly in busy periods.
keyNumbers: Climbs about 160 m

parts.description: Enclosed observation deck at 276 m, with an open-air level above it.

details.didYouKnow: The top floor is the highest observation deck open to the public in the European Union.
details.howItWorks: The top floor has an enclosed, glazed level with a panoramic view and a smaller open-air level above it behind safety mesh. It sits where the four upper girders meet, so it is supported from all corners. Visitors also find a champagne bar and Eiffel's restored apartment here.
keyNumbers: About 276 m above the ground
View reaching tens of km on a clear day
Roughly 6 to 7 million visitors to the tower a year

parts.description: Small private apartment Eiffel built for himself at the top, now restored with wax figures of him and Thomas Edison.

details.didYouKnow: When Thomas Edison visited in 1889 he gave Eiffel one of his phonographs, and the wax figures show the two men together.
details.howItWorks: Eiffel built this small apartment for himself near the summit and used it to entertain distinguished guests and to work. Next to it were rooms used for scientific observations, such as weather measurements. Today visitors look in through windows at a recreated scene with wax figures.
keyNumbers: About 276 m above Paris
Thomas Edison visited in about 1889

details.howItWorks: The lantern sits above the top floor and carries the beacon whose beams sweep across Paris at night. The lamps turn so the beams rotate like a lighthouse. It also supports equipment that leads up to the antenna mast.

summary: The 330 m wrought-iron tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, built by Gustave Eiffel's company for the 1889 World's Fair: about 18,000 iron pieces held together by some 2.5 million rivets.
